title: Die Geschichte vom Zappel-Philipp
source: Heinrich Hoffmann, Der Struwwelpeter, Rütten & Loening, Frankfurt am Main, 564. Auflage — the canonical later text in modernized spelling (via Project Gutenberg #24571). Fresh Lectorium translation from the German.
about: Philipp cannot sit still at table. His father does not order him to — he wonders aloud, in a serious tone, whether the boy will manage it today; his mother says nothing at all and only looks round the table; and Philipp rocks his chair until the whole dinner comes down on top of him. The verse fidgets where he does — the lines shrink to two words apiece — and the poem breaks off to point at Hoffmann’s picture on the page above. The ending is not a punishment but a wrecked meal and two angry, hungry parents.

sentences.t:
»Ob der Philipp heute still
wohl bei Tische sitzen will?«
sentences.l:
“Whether the Philipp today quiet
perhaps at table sit will?”
sentences.i:
“Is Philipp going to sit still
at table today, I wonder?”
sentences.n: A question that is really a wondering-aloud: a clause beginning »Ob …?« and standing on its own means ‘I wonder whether …’, and »wohl« adds exactly that shade. Being a subordinate clause, it holds its verb (»will«) to the very end. »still« is ‘quiet, motionless’ and never English ‘still’; »still sitzen« = ‘to sit quietly, sit still.’ »bei Tische« is the old dative -e preserved in a fixed phrase. And »der Philipp« — the article before the name once more.

sentences.t:
Also sprach in ernstem Ton
der Papa zu seinem Sohn,
und die Mutter blickte stumm
auf dem ganzen Tisch herum.
sentences.l:
Thus spoke in earnest tone
the papa to his son,
and the mother looked mutely
over the whole table around.
sentences.i:
So spoke, in a serious tone,
the papa to his son,
and the mother looked in silence
all round the table.
sentences.n: »also« is the old ‘thus, so’ (as in »Also sprach Zarathustra«), nothing to do with English ‘also.’ »sprach« is the storybook past again. »herumblicken« is separable, and the frame »auf … herum« wraps round the noun: ‘around over the whole table,’ with the »herum« waiting at the very end. »stumm« is ‘mute, without speaking’ — the mother never says a word in this poem; she only looks, and her two lines come back after the crash with nothing changed but the tense.

sentences.t:
Doch der Philipp hörte nicht,
was zu ihm der Vater spricht.
sentences.l:
But the Philipp heard not,
what to him the father speaks.
sentences.i:
But Philipp paid no attention
to what his father was saying.
sentences.n: »hören« covers both ‘hear’ and ‘listen’; here it is plainly the second — not deafness but disregard. The tenses slip mid-sentence, past »hörte« and then present »spricht«, half for the rhyme and half because the storyteller keeps stepping into the scene. In the »was«-clause the verb goes last.

sentences.t:
Er gaukelt
und schaukelt,
er trappelt
und zappelt
auf dem Stuhle hin und her.
sentences.l:
He flits
and rocks,
he patters
and fidgets
on the chair to and fro.
sentences.i:
He flutters
and rocks,
he drums his feet
and wriggles
to and fro on his chair.
sentences.n: The lines break down to two words apiece and the rhythm itself begins to fidget — the shape on the page is doing the boy’s work. »gaukeln« is to flit or waver unsteadily (the word behind »Gaukler«, a tumbler or juggler); »schaukeln« is to swing or rock; »trappeln« is the patter of quick feet; »zappeln« is to wriggle and squirm — the verb he is named for. »auf dem Stuhle« has the old dative -e again.

»mißfallen« puts the person in the dative: the thing displeases *to* someone, »das mißfällt mir«. »sehr« keeps its old force here, ‘greatly, sorely’ — the same use as Konrad’s »schreit sehr«. »mißfällt« is the pre-reform spelling of »missfällt«.

sentences.t:
Seht, ihr lieben Kinder, seht,
wie's dem Philipp weiter geht!
sentences.l:
See, you dear children, see,
how it to-the Philipp further goes!
sentences.i:
Look, dear children, look
at how Philipp fares from here!
sentences.n: »seht« is the plural imperative: the poem turns from the story and speaks straight to the children listening. »wie es jemandem geht« is the ordinary idiom for how someone is doing (»wie geht’s?«), with the person in the dative — »dem Philipp« — and »weiter« adding ‘on, from here.’ »wie’s« = »wie es«.

sentences.t: Oben steht es auf dem Bild.
sentences.l: Above stands it on the picture.
sentences.i: It is up there in the picture.
sentences.n: The verse points at Hoffmann’s own illustration on the same page — in this book the pictures carry part of the telling, and the words expect you to look. German says a thing »steht« (stands) on a picture or a page where English would say it simply ‘is’ there.

sentences.t:
Seht! er schaukelt gar zu wild,
bis der Stuhl nach hinten fällt.
sentences.l:
See! he rocks even too wildly,
until the chair to-behind falls.
sentences.i:
Look! he rocks far too wildly,
until the chair goes over backwards.
sentences.n: »gar zu« = ‘far too, altogether too,’ with »gar« doing the intensifying. »nach hinten« = ‘backwards, to the rear.’ In the »bis«-clause the verb »fällt« goes to the end, so the fall arrives, in German, as the last word.

sentences.t: Da ist nichts mehr, was ihn hält.
sentences.l: There is nothing more, that him holds.
sentences.i: There is nothing left to hold him.
sentences.n: »nichts mehr« = ‘nothing any more, nothing left.’ After »nichts« German uses »was« as its relative pronoun (not »das«), and the verb »hält« goes to the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Nach dem Tischtuch greift er, schreit.
sentences.l: For the tablecloth grabs he, screams.
sentences.i: He grabs at the tablecloth, and screams.
sentences.n: »greifen nach« is ‘to reach for, grab at’; the »nach«-phrase is thrown to the front here, which pushes the verb into second place and the subject behind it. The bare »schreit« — no »und«, no repeated »er« — is the poem’s shorthand for how fast this is happening.

sentences.t:
Doch was hilft's? Zu gleicher Zeit
fallen Teller, Flasch und Brot.
sentences.l:
But what helps it? At same time
fall plates, bottle and bread.
sentences.i:
But what good is that? At that same moment
down come the plates, the bottle and the bread.
sentences.n: »was hilft’s?« (= »was hilft es?«) is a set turn: ‘what use is it?’ — the narrator shrugging in the middle of the disaster. »zu gleicher Zeit« takes the first slot of the next sentence, so the verb »fallen« comes straight after it and the falling things stack up behind. »Flasch« is »Flasche« clipped for the meter, like »Scher« and »Stub« before it.

sentences.t:
Vater ist in großer Not,
und die Mutter blicket stumm
auf dem ganzen Tisch herum.
sentences.l:
Father is in great distress,
and the mother looks mutely
over the whole table around.
sentences.i:
Father is in great distress,
and the mother looks in silence
all round the table.
sentences.n: »Not« is ‘distress, straits’ (the word the Friederich’s cats suffered). »blicket« is the older full form of »blickt«, kept for the meter — and note the tense: the first time she »blickte«, past, and now she »blicket«, present, the poem stepping into the scene. Otherwise her two lines return exactly as before: she looked round the table before the crash and she looks round it after, and that is the whole of her part.

sentences.t:
Nun ist Philipp ganz versteckt,
und der Tisch ist abgedeckt.
sentences.l:
Now is Philipp quite hidden,
and the table is off-covered.
sentences.i:
Now Philipp is hidden completely,
and the table is cleared.
sentences.n: The rhyme carries the joke: »abdecken« (separable — »ist abgedeckt«) is the everyday word for clearing the table after a meal, except that here the cloth and everything on it have gone off in one pull. Philipp is »versteckt«, hidden — buried under the wreck of the meal.

sentences.t:
Was der Vater essen wollt,
unten auf der Erde rollt.
sentences.l:
What the father eat wanted,
below on the ground rolls.
sentences.i:
What the father meant to eat
is rolling about on the floor.
sentences.n: A relative clause standing in for the subject: ‘(that) which the father wanted to eat.’ Both clauses end on their verbs (»wollt«, »rollt«), which is what makes the rhyme. »wollt« is »wollte« clipped. »die Erde« here is the ground or floor, not ‘the earth.’

sentences.t:
Suppe, Brot und alle Bissen,
alles ist herabgerissen.
sentences.l:
Soup, bread and all morsels,
everything is down-torn.
sentences.i:
Soup, bread and every last mouthful —
all of it dragged down.
sentences.n: »herabreißen« = ‘to tear down’ (»herab«, down from up there); in the past participle the »ge-« slips inside the compound, »herab-ge-rissen«. »der Bissen« is a bite or mouthful, from »beißen« (to bite). The things are listed first and then gathered up by »alles« — a common German turn, and here it lands like the crash itself.

sentences.t:
Suppenschüssel ist entzwei,
und die Eltern stehn dabei.
sentences.l:
Soup-tureen is in-two,
and the parents stand by.
sentences.i:
The soup tureen is in two pieces,
and the parents stand there beside it.
sentences.n: »entzwei« means ‘broken, in pieces’ — literally ‘in two,’ still audible in »entzweigehen«. The article is dropped before »Suppenschüssel« for the meter. »dabeistehen« is ‘to stand by’; »stehn« is »stehen« clipped. The parents do nothing whatever — standing by is their entire contribution.

sentences.t:
Beide sind gar zornig sehr,
haben nichts zu essen mehr.
sentences.l:
Both are even angry sorely,
have nothing to eat more.
sentences.i:
Both of them are very angry indeed,
and have nothing left to eat.
sentences.n: »gar … sehr« piles one intensifier on another, and »sehr« again carries its older weight, ‘sorely.’ The last line drops its subject (»sie haben«) — verse shorthand. And there the poem stops: no punishment, no repentance, only a ruined dinner and two hungry parents.
